rationale: B wins because it keeps the same strong four story shapes without letting the trend angle outrun the evidence. A's line, "Bumble is the highest-profile dating platform to deploy AI matchmaking and AI-assisted message writing at scale," is invented bravado; B's line, "Caution: Bumble cannot credibly own a \"whole industry\" trend claim on these facts alone," is the adult in the room. The best angle in both sets is the women-first/AI tension, but B frames it as a product-design question instead of reaching for "Still Feminist?" before the proof is in.
gaps_in_A: "Bumble is the highest-profile dating platform to deploy AI matchmaking and AI-assisted message writing at scale" invents scale and competitive status. The update gives neither.

"Users Push Back as Dating Apps Embrace AI Matchmaking" overbuilds a category trend from one company relaunch and vague user criticism. The set admits it needs outside research, which means the headline is ahead of the evidence.
"Is Bumble's Women-First Model Still Feminist?" imports a feminism frame the update does not supply. The real angle is women-message-first versus AI-assisted authorship; don't decorate it.
"the relaunch is the stated answer to the subscriber slide" is too strong. The facts say the relaunch follows declining paying users, not that Bumble explicitly positioned it as the answer.
gaps_in_B: "the \"founder-as-turnaround\" pattern (the Dorsey/Schultz/Kalanick-adjacent storyline)" is showy comparison bait. It may help a strategist think, but it is not grounded in the Bumble facts and risks sending the pitch sideways.
"A founder who stepped back is back as CEO to fix the company she built" makes motive and success sound cleaner than the evidence. Make it "try to fix" or keep it as a question.
"major public dating company" is probably defensible, but it is still an unsourced adjective. "Publicly traded dating company" carries the story without puffing it.
The authenticity-trend proof list asks for "any data on opt-in/usage" but should also demand named, sourced user complaints. The update's "some users" is too thin for a culture piece.
